Cloud computing firm Megaspeed has come under fresh scrutiny as the US looks into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy .
Nvidia has seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped from its value in recent days after the US chipmaker said it would investigate Huang’s admitted relationship with the former Megaspeed director Alice Huang .
China says allegations about Chinese spies are “entirely groundless” and “intended to smear and malign China”. But US intelligence officials nevertheless believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was funneling information to Beijing .
For years, Washington has tried to keep China from gaining the know-how to rival the United States in cutting-edge AI, which Nvidia’s chips support.
Now attention turns to Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Beijing ‌gain access ⁠to advanced AI chips whose export to China is restricted.
Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International before changing its name to Megaspeed International in March 2023, when it was bought by a British Virgin Islands company called Huang Le Ltd.
Alice Huang ended her eight month tenure as managing director months later, in October 2023, but is reported to still be involved in the company. In November 2023, the firm was sold again to a Singaporean entity called Swiftdata, which says its main job is providing hosting services by non-data centres.
Megaspeed's assets increased sharply to $3 billion in 2024 from $33 million in 2023, its business filings showed.
The company soon became one of Nvidia’s biggest Asian customers and grew rapidly as a link between the US chipmaker and the Chinese tech group Alibaba. Two Singapore citizens are listed as officers of both Megaspeed and Swiftdata.
Singapore has come under mounting pressure from the US to clamp down on companies suspected of transferring advanced AI chips to Chinese firms. But the city-state does not necessarily exclude such transfers.
Singaporean police are now conducting their own investigation into Megaspeed, in step with US authorities. US intelligence officials have already concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to the New York Times .
US intelligence officials have reportedly been alert to Alice Huang’s position for some time. According to the New York Times , US president Donald Trump was briefed on intelligence findings around a year ago but chose to do nothing with them.
It was late last year that US authorities began investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it was helping to divert Nvidia chips to China.
Singapore police said they would investigate the firm over “suspected breaches of our domestic laws” after a US senator asked the commerce department to look into related concerns.
According to the NYT, officials suspected it was Alice Huang who was feeding information directly to Beijing on how to gain access to the advanced AI chips.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and told the newspaper that it was “committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations” and would welcome a “formal, evidence-based investigation”.
It said in a statement last year that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities”.
And Nvidia said Megaspeed was just like any other regional customer, and that such customers only “receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security”.
For all the concerns above, the affair between Alice Huang and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has rocked the tech and political worlds. It remains unclear how long the affair lasted, and when exactly the relationship might have ended.
Alice Huang was a Chinese finance executive before becoming involved in artificial intelligence, data centers and computer chips. She became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder in March 2023, according to research by the C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on global security.
But by November 2023, she was no longer listed as a director, and all her shares were transferred to a Singaporean businessman, Tan Yong Pong, who also is known as James Tan.
While public records suggest Alice Huang left Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research issued a report in May this year that cited a Megaspeed employee saying Huang was “actually still our boss” and was still involved in the company’s daily operations.
Before Megaspeed, Alice Huang previously held senior positions at the Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database.
Before that, she worked at HSBC’s Hong Kong private banking arm and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo returns to what is expected to be a national party in his second homeland of Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo returns to what is expected to be a national party in his second homeland of Peru
articles.content_orig:
Today, Pope Leo XIV sets out on the third and final leg of this long journey in Latin America. He will fly 2,200 miles from Buenos Aires to Lima, the capital of Peru, a multi-ethnic nation of almost 35 million people.
Leo has dreamed of making this visit since his election on May 8, 2025. He is the third pope to visit Peru after St. John Paul II (1985) and Pope Francis (2018), but the first to do so as a citizen of the country. He became a citizen in 2015 when Pope Francis appointed him bishop of Chiclayo.
His arrival in Peru will be a homecoming. He spent more than 20 years as a missionary in the country. “He is so excited” to return to this land that “was so important to his ministry,” the new prefect of Vatican communications, Maria Montserrat “Montse” Alvarado, told journalists at a press briefing on Nov. 3. Ms. Alvarado is accompanying him on this 12-day journey in Latin America as part of Leo’s Vatican entourage.
Robert Prevost first came to Peru in 1985 as an Augustinian missionary priest serving in Chulucanas; he later worked in Trujillo and Piura. Indeed, he has spent half of his priestly life working in Peru. He served as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, when Francis called him to Rome to serve as prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and soon after made him cardinal.
Catholicism has deep roots in Peru, where some 76 percent of its population identifies as Catholic. But Vatican statistics show a significant decline in baptisms and religious weddings between 1980 and 2024, and Leo is likely to seek to give new life to the faith in Peru, as he did in Uruguay and Argentina .
The Catholic Church is carrying out its ministry in a politically unstable and polarized country, marked by widespread corruption. Though rich in resources, Peru’s national poverty level stood at over 25 percent in 2025, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Informatics. This means almost nine million Peruvians are living in poverty, concentrated in metropolitan Lima and Callao.
Since Pope Francis visited Peru in January 2018, its political landscape has been marked by institutional instability, with a rapid turnover of presidents—eight since that visit. There has been intense conflict between the executive and legislative branches of government and systemic corruption scandals, amid growing public protests.
The current right-wing, tough-on-crime president, Keiko Fujimori, was elected in June and will welcome Leo on his arrival. She is the daughter of the authoritarian leader Alberto Fujimori, who served as president from 1990 to 2000 and was later imprisoned for human rights abuses.
The first Augustinian pope will spend six full days in Peru and visit four cities: Lima, the capital city, where he will reside at the Vatican embassy; Chiclayo, the diocese in northwestern Peru where he was bishop (his returns there on Nov. 13., the anniversary of the birth of St. Augustine, and the celebration of all the saints of his order); Cuzco, a city at 11,000 feet above sea level in the central Peruvian Andes that was once the heart of the Inca Empire; and Pucallpa, a city in the Amazonian forest in eastern Peru.
On arrival at Lima’s Callao Air Base, he will be welcomed by Ms. Fujimori. He will have a private conversation with her at the government palace before addressing a gathering of state authorities, representatives of civil society and the diplomatic corps. There is great interest in what he will say to the Peruvian officials. Rich in natural resources, the nation is plagued by corruption, political instability and poverty. Many Peruvians are trapped working in the gig economy.
On Nov. 12, Leo will meet  Peruvian bishops at the archbishop’s residence in Lima. Afterward, he will celebrate the midday prayer in the Cathedral of St. John the Apostle and Evangelist with the bishops, accompanied by Peru’s clergy, women and men religious, seminarians, synodal teams and pastoral council members. From there, he will go to the square in front of the cathedral for a public meeting on “the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people,” attended by families and people from the world of culture and business.
In the afternoon, he will meet with members of the Augustinian order in Peru before presiding at a prayer vigil with young people and college students at the national soccer stadium. Leo will conclude the day by dining with the bishops at the Vatican embassy.
On Friday morning, Nov. 13, he will fly from Lima to the coastal city of Chiclayo in northwest Peru, where he will be welcomed by the Augustinian bishop Edinson Edgardo Farfán Córdova who was close to then-Robert Francis Prevost when Leo served there as bishop.
Chiclayo was founded in the 16th century and today is Peru’s fourth most populous city, with a population of around 690,000. Chiclayo is a financial and commercial hub. He will spend two nights in the bishop’s residence, where he lived for over eight years while serving as bishop.
Soon after his arrival, he will celebrate Mass at the Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert flatland near the city. He will then drive nine miles to pray in the Chapel of St. Óscar Romero in the La Victoria neighborhood of Chiclayo. He has a particular devotion to that community and to the martyred bishop revered for defending the poor against military repression in El Salvador. Leo carries a prayer card and relic of the saint with him. Bishop Prevost secured funds from the church in the United States to rebuild what was once a dilapidated chapel here.
Later in the afternoon, he will address a gathering of clergy, religious and lay people at the large Shrine of Our Lady of Peace. Afterward, he will meet staff and students of the Santo Toribio de Mongrovejo Catholic University, which was opened in 1998 and is sponsored by the bishop of Chiclayo. He will conclude the day at dinner with the priests of the Diocese of Chiclayo at the College of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.
On the morning of Nov. 14, Leo will begin the day by crowning the statue of the Immaculate Virgin in the Cathedral of Saint Mary before taking a helicopter to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, the capital of Santa Cruz province at an elevation of 6,500 feet, to celebrate Mass. He will be the first pope to visit there.
That evening, back in Chiclayo, he will preside at a prayer meeting with the Catholic community for the closing of the Jubilee Year of St. Turibius de Mogrovejo, the saintly Spanish missionary bishop who proclaimed the Gospel in Peru and was archbishop of Lima from 1579 to his death in 1606.
On his penultimate day here, Sunday, Nov. 15, Pope Leo will take a flight to Cuzco, the ancient capital of the Inca Empire in the Andes. As a missionary, he learned Quechua, the indigenous language of the Inca people, by listening to and speaking with the local people.
On arrival at Cuzco, he will meet the faithful and representatives of popular devotion at the Saqsaywaman National Archaeological Park and later pray the Angelus in the square in front of the Cathedral of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
In the afternoon, he will fly from Cuzco to Pucallpa, a city on the Ucayali River in the Amazonian rainforest of eastern Peru that has long been a center of Catholic missionary work. He will meet with missionaries and representatives of the Amazonian peoples at the Callao Port Terminal and afterward celebrate Mass in the city’s sports complex.
That evening, he will fly back to Lima and spend his last night in Peru at the nunciature.
On Monday morning, Nov. 16, he will be driven to the nearby port city of Callao. There he will visit a shelter for abandoned elderly people run by the Little Sisters, before celebrating Mass at the Las Palmas Air Base.
Ms. Fujimori will bid him farewell at the air base before he boards the plane for the nearly 15-hour flight back to Rome, during which he will hold a press conference.
He is scheduled to arrive back at Rome’s Leonardo Da Vinci airport at 10:25 a.m. local time o

articles.title_orig: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
articles.title_zh: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
articles.content_orig:
Poundland looks set to avoid immediate collapse after its US owners told MPs on Wednesday they were in favour of extending a deadline to find a rescue deal.
The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by Gordon Borthers from accessing cash in its bank accounts.
A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation told the BBC they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding.
A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.
Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.
The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims.
But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.
However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of £10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored.
Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street".
"They refused to prioritise, protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he added.
"It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge."
Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year".
He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now".
"It's a good business, it's a much-loved business, and particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added.
Following the private meeting with MPs, Poundland's chief executive Barry Williams told the BBC the chain's board would hold an urgent meeting on Wednesday night.
The 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires on Thursday, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.
Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners.
Poundland boss Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.
He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m.
However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It has argued the best way of securing jobs may be to split up the business and sell chunks of its 600 sites to other retailers.
There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up.
The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain.

articles.title_orig: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
articles.title_zh: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
articles.content_orig:
The Home Assistant Connect Aux-2 helped me track my fridge temperature and finally set up my in-wall speakers.﻿

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation , which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2 , a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly . And it’s working.
I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. It has 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB-A, USB-C, a digital/analog audio jack, a Grove port for interfacing with peripherals like sensors, buttons, and LEDs , and a pair of RS-232 serial ports.
It can bridge Bluetooth devices into your Home Assistant setup. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. You can control devices like TVs, AV receivers, solar inverters, and more via serial connector. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment.
All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome , an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year ; Music Assistant and SendSpin , which power the audio-out feature, are in active development.
I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. The situation is not ideal.
But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. I want to know when that happens before all my food goes bad.
A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle , and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers , but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. That happens to be a feature of the Aux-2.
I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. I’d been meaning to get an amp, but analysis paralysis set in. Do I get a Wiim Amp? A stereo receiver? A cheap Bluetooth amp? Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Maybe my ancient Google Home speaker? Turns out I do nothing for five years. Maybe the Aux-2 could help.
Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. I plugged it into my computer via USB-C and was able to download and install the latest firmware right from a browser. I could also add my Wi-Fi credentials. Then I unplugged it, moved it over to my media console and connected it to power (it takes USB-C or power over Ethernet), and did the rest of the setup in the Home Assistant interface.
In HA, I was prompted to install ESPHome, which discovered the Aux-2 and sent me to a “set up your ESPHome device page” that walked me through the capabilities. Enabling Bluetooth proxying took a couple of clicks; I added the Govee Bluetooth integration and put batteries into the sensors and they showed up automatically. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again.
The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant , which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. Not a long beat: less than half an hour total.
I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin , the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The standard is still in development, and I’ve also been busy, so I’m not sure if that’s a me problem or a them problem.
I would also like to see the Aux-2 show up as an AirPlay or Spotify Connect target, which (again) is probably just a thing I need to set up.
Serial control is the most intriguing feature of the Aux-2, and it’s unfortunately the thing I haven’t yet had time to test. But the ability to hook in things like solar inverters, TVs, and receivers is fascinating and one I want to look into further when I get the chance. Maybe I’ll hook it up to my LG TV.
The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1 , for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts.
That’s not a knock against the Aux-2. That’s the whole point . The ecosystem is open by design, which I find endlessly refreshing. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. But there’s nothing stopping you from making your own devices. It’s actively encouraged.
I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. I could have built a Bluetooth proxy from one of those. I could have built an LED controller. I could have built a soil sensor, or a media player, or any of a dozen other things. I didn’t do anything at all.
But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump says Iran war will be over "when we want to end it"
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest U.S. official to be threatened or targeted by Iran, but he is far from the first.
The Iranian regime has been implicated in various plots to target top U.S. officials since 2020, when President Trump ordered the killing of Iranian general Qassem Soleimani .
Threats against Americans have ramped up since the start of the war with Iran. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in October that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
U.S. households are expected to face higher costs this winter to warm their homes, especially those depending on heating oil, according to a new forecast.
Winter heating costs are expected to average $1,002 for all fuels for the season, up 7.1% from last winter, according to projections released this week from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association.
But a much sharper increase will hit properties reliant on home heating oil , a particularly popular source in the Northeast for which prices have swelled due to the Iran war.
Those households will pay $2,977 this winter, up 70.2% from last year.
The association pointed to declines in home heating prices in recent weeks, but "families should not assume that prices will continue to fall," said executive director Mark Wolfe.
Nationwide, more than 4 million households use heating oil as their primary fuel source, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, and of those, 82% are concentrated in the Northeast.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for dialogue and restraint to ease regional tensions during a meeting Wednesday with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, according to Sharif's office.
Sharif expressed deep concern over the prolonged conflict as the two spoke on the sidelines of the United Nations climate summit in Turkey, his office said. The prime minister stressed the need to build on an interim deal reached between the U.S. and Iran in June.
In August, Pezeshkian described the deal as the best way for Iran to move on from a situation that he described as "neither war nor peace."
President Trump said Wednesday the U.S. has already won the war against Iran, but when the conflict will end is a different question.
"America did not start a war with Iran," he said at a Veterans Day event at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. "Iran has been waging war on America since 1979. This should have been taken care of a long time ago."
"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back," he continued. "All of us fought back. We fought back. And we seriously fought back. And we won. Just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory. It's going to be total. It'll take them 25 years to rebuild back what we have destroyed, and hopefully we won't have to destroy any more of that country."
The president reminded Americans that the Korean War lasted much longer and cost more lives, as did the Vietnam War and the Iraq War.
As he has been saying for months, Mr. Trump said the conflict will be over soon.
Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to strike U.S. bases beyond the Middle East, including in Europe, if they are used for attacks against the Islamic Republic.
"If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well," Rezaei told Lebanon-based Al Mayadeen TV in an interview broadcast Wednesday.
In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday, President Trump said he does not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war.
Rezaei also said that Iran's response to renewed U.S. attacks would "target America's more distant military installations — including the ones we have not yet attacked," without specifying.
"We may even strike certain islands that they assume are beyond the reach of our missiles," he added during the interview, which was conducted in Tehran.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday that it shot down three cruise missiles fired at Riyadh, which has been targeted for weeks by the Iran-backed group.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed 3 cruise missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki posted on social media.
The latest incident comes after the Houthis damaged a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco in the capital's gleaming financial district on Sunday.
Riyadh's international airport has also been targeted repeatedly, with deadly attacks forcing it to close for two weeks last month.
Saudi Arabia formed an international coalition to fight the Houthis in 2015, after the group's takeover of Yemen's capital Sanaa.
After years of an uneasy truce, the conflict reignited in July.
Iran's Defense Ministry on Wednesday rejected Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's latest blustery assessment of Tehran's military capacities, calling his depiction a fabrication and insisting Iranian armed forces still had weapons stockpiled.
Iran's weapons stockpile "far exceeds the deceptive figures fabricated by Trump and the defeated Pete," a ministry spokesperson said, adding that the country had made use of "strategic production and upgraded technologies."
Hegseth told reporters Tuesday that during 40 days of combat, the U.S. had struck 13,000 targets, destroying, he said, more than 80% of Iran's nuclear industrial base.
"Their navy sunk, their air force grounded, their defense industrial base gone," Hegseth said.
Iranian officials claimed a month ago that the country's weapons production capacity had increased by 250% since the war began, with help from Russia and China.
Neither side has offered evidence to prove their claims, and neither the U.S. nor Iran have launched large-scale strikes since the summer. Both claim to have won the war, but despite Hegseth's assertion on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz is under U.S. control, Iran continues attacking vessels daily in and near the waterway.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life.
"The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said.
A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move.
"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the U.S. on Wednesday of threatening to attack his country with America's largest non-nuclear weapon — the "mother of all bombs" — while claiming to seek a diplomatic resolution to the war.
In a post on X , Pezeshkian criticized the U.S. for what he called an effort to "pursue diplomacy through threats."
"No contradiction but a disgrace. Who threatens global peace and security?" he wrote.
CBS News reported in October that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB — an acronym that has earned it the nickname used by Pezeshkian —   to hit military sites in Iran if President Trump were to give the order, according to sources familiar with the matter.

articles.title_orig: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.title_zh: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.content_orig:
Authorities in Spain say that despite pouring rain, some 120,000 citizens took to the streets of the capital, Madrid, on Wednesday evening after millions of striking workers brought Europe's fourth-largest economy to a standstill under the motto "Salaries. Housing. Prices" in the country's first general strike in 14 years earlier in the day.
The massive turnout came in response to housing shortages and unbearably high rents.
City officials in Barcelona said 55,000 people attended evening marches there as they walked behind a huge banner reading "Live. Not just survive." Housing activists in the city said the turnout was far larger, claiming that 400,000 had hit the streets.
As has been the case in other demonstrations across the Europea of late , peaceful protests later gave way to small groups of marauding young men who smashed storefront windows along Barcelona's main shopping street. They also set fire to dumpsters and shot fireworks at police when they arrived.
Earlier on Wednesday, workers across Spain gathered en masse, marching and setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in many areas of the country.
Symbolized by the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid earlier this year, the crisis has also prompted a snap election set for November 29.
The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass legislation to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. Lacking the power to get legislation passed, Sanchez called the early vote in hopes of shoring up more support.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Sanchez's government did end up approving two extraordinary decrees introducing measures similar to the housing reforms rejected by parliament.
"We won't stop until we transform this country's housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the [landlord] minority," said Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union.
While most of the protests were peaceful, strikers in front of Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market said police had used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention.
Some airlines later reported disruptions to flights in and out of Spain as some airport and airline workers participated in the strike.
The country has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set ​to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to estimates from the central bank.
With fewer and fewer individuals and families able to buy a home, the number of renters in the country has risen sharply. According to Spain's youth council, the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315). This is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary.
The general strike came a day after rail workers launched a strike over two major deadly train crashes this year, making decrepit infrastructure another major issue in the upcoming parliamentary elections.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Spain's government supported Wednesday's strike, saying it was staged "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition."
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), had a different take, saying if it was indeed "a strike against the opposition," it was "an absurdity the likes of which does not exist in any other European Union country."
Although the UGT labor union — one of the strike organizers — and Sanchez's socialist PSOE party are two separate institutions, they share a historic founder in Pablo Iglesias Posse.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Nicole Ris, reporting for DW in Madrid, followed the strike closely as it unfolded on Wednesday, saying earlier:
Here in Madrid, apparently, lots of people are still showing up for work, and people I know have clearly said they will not go on strike as they don't see much sense in it — although they all suffer under the cost of living crisis and the housing crisis.
There is also debate about this strike being an "election strike" that could benefit the current government.
"I'm not taking part in this. It's nonsense. The government is supporting it because they hope they'll get enough votes on the 29th so they can carry on," a doorman in Madrid told me.
The government supports the strike, claiming it is being held "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez's inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition," according to the media here.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks rose on Wednesday, but a series of bombshell reports after the closing bell took the spotlight as the New York Times reported Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has had a second extramarital affair with an Nvidia exec, followed by a second story from the Wall Street Journal that the company's board is preparing to oust Huang .
Follow our live blog on the stories here.
As Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) hotly anticipated IPO draws nearer, the AI trade remains front and center, particularly after the midterm elections have brought the country to a crossroads on the data center build-out.
The stock market was open on Veterans Day ; however, the bond market was closed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.5%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) climbed 1.3%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) added 1.6%, officially erasing its post-election losses as of Wednesday's close.
CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock surged 24% after the company reported a better-than-expected revenue outlook on the back of strong AI compute demand.
Otherwise, it was a quiet day on the earnings and economic data front as traders recalibrated their bets for higher interest rates following hotter-than-expected CPI inflation data .
Embattled Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang was allegedly involved in a second extramarital affair.
The company's board is reportedly meeting to determine if it will oust Huang as chief executive, the Wall Street Journal reports . Nvidia stock fell in after-hours trading following the report.
According to the New York Times , Huang, whose relationship with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy has embroiled the company in scandal this week, also had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell.
She joined Nvidia in 2008 and heads up the company's healthcare business.
The Times report says that Huang and Powell were seen being affectionate at a hotel during a company conference in March, and that when a bystander took a photo of the interaction, a security guard "sequestered them" and made them an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement.
Semiconductors led a stock market rally on Wednesday after CoreWeave's better-than-expected earnings reignited the AI trade.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.5%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) climbed 1.3%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) added 1.6%, officially erasing its post-election losses on Wednesday.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) snapped a two-day losing streak, gaining more than 3%. Shares of chipmakers AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) also rallied. Storage maker Sandisk ( SNDK ) and memory chipmakers Micron Technology ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) all gained more than 10%.
Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) gained more than 1% to hover near $74,500 per token on Wednesday as investors went risk-on.
Technology stocks led the market gains, while crypto prices also bumped higher. Ether ( ETH-USD ) also jumped 1% to hold above $2,000 per token.
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports:
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) loyal investor base is starting to get antsy about the endgame for newly embattled CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang admitted to the affair on Sunday in an email to employees. Nvidia stock is down about 12% since the situation became public.
"At this point, the market is pricing in two major potential headwinds," strategists at the Kobeissi Letter said. "First, the growing possibility that Jensen Huang will be removed as CEO. Second, [the] possibility that sensitive Nvidia technology or information was compromised."
Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent investigation into reports that the woman Huang had an affair with was allegedly a spy for the Chinese government.
Yahoo Finance's Page Oamek reports:
AI power-provider stocks rallied on Wednesday after CoreWeave ( CRWV ) posted earnings that eased worries about how data center build-outs get funded. Bloom Energy ( BE ) was one of the biggest winners, jumping about 16% by midday.
The move may not have been a total surprise.
Bloom's third quarter earnings, announced in late October, were a mixed picture. On one hand, the company, which designs, manufactures, and installs solid oxide fuel cells, reported record revenue of $1.24 billion, up 138% from a year earlier, and raised its 2026 revenue guidance for the third time this year, to $4.4 billion to $4.6 billion. It was also added to the S&P 500.
On the other hand, Bloom burned cash. Operating cash flow was negative $27.1 million, and capital expenditures rose to $153.5 million, nearly triple its second quarter capex.
Still, management said the market is broadening.
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
Wall Street analysts have rapidly adjusted their forecasts after the third straight month of bad inflation news.
The affordability crunch featured as a core issue steering voters in the midterm elections. And those frustrations were echoed in the latest inflation data, showing price increases in food, rent, medical care, and electronics.
As Bank of America analysts put it in a note on Tuesday, "goods prices are becoming a problem (again)," and the recent inflation firmness is spreading to more things that Americans both need and want to buy.
Wall Street has already figured that rising costs have all but secured another rate hike in December. But the fresh inflation numbers were so discouraging that analysts are changing their projections or contemplating more and bigger rate hikes.
Everyday investors could pour a record $250 million into Anthropic shares on its first trading day, according to Vanda Research.
The estimate, which would be more than double the $118 million in net retail buying the first day of SpaceX's June listing, hinges on a surge in derivatives trading tied to Anthropic's yet-to-be listed shares on crypto exchange Hyperliquid.
Trading volume in this Anthropic-linked instrument reached a record $270 million on Tuesday, nearly triple last week's daily volumes, according to Vanda strategist Viraj Patel.
Vanda found that retail stock trading activity on the opening days of recent IPOs, including SpaceX, was roughly five times the peak daily trading volume in their pre-IPO derivatives. Applied to Anthropic, the assessment would suggest $250 million in net buying on its listing day planned for next week.
The projection carries considerable uncertainty. The derivatives trading represents an indirect gauge of investor enthusiasm, and patterns from previous IPOs may not repeat.
Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $1.4 trillion, below the $2 trillion previously discussed, as the AI industry has faced headwinds from rising borrowing costs, hedge fund deleveraging, and political backlash over data center construction.
CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock extended gains in midday trading on Wednesday, surging as much as 25% after the AI infrastructure provider raised its revenue outlook and prepayments, helping ease concerns about its ability to finance its rapid expansion.
The company also said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, and said it does not plan to take on more expensive debt through 2027, easing concerns about how it will fund its expansion.
CoreWeave shares have been battered in recent weeks amid concerns about rising financing costs and its debt-heavy balance sheet. Its bonds have sold off sharply, underscoring investor concerns about the cost of funding its expansion.
Quantum-related stocks moved in different directions on Wednesday after D-Wave Quantum ( QBTS ) and Rigetti Computing ( RGTI ) posted third quarter results.
After the close on Tuesday, Rigetti stock fell on an earnings miss and fears of elevated capital expenditures. The company reported an adjusted loss per share of $0.06, compared to estimates for a $0.05 loss. Similarly, D-Wave fell short of analysts' consensus earnings per share estimate, posting an adjusted loss per share of $0.13 versus analysts' estimate of a $0.10 loss.

articles.title_orig: Why Nvidia Stock Rose Today Despite Calls for CEO Jensen Huang to Step Down
articles.title_zh: Why Nvidia Stock Rose Today Despite Calls for CEO Jensen Huang to Step Down
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Nvidia fell more than 7% in after-hours trading on Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that the company's board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang .
The news landed minutes after The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with another executive at the company.
The alleged relationship was with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia, according to the report. Powell's bio on the Nvidia website says she's "responsible for the company's worldwide healthcare business, including hardware and software platforms for accelerated computing, AI, and visualization that power the ecosystem of medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery, and healthcare analytics."
Huang and Powell were reportedly captured on camera being affectionate with one another at a hotel in San Jose, California in March, according to the Times.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, according to The Financial Times , who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported.
Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into the spying allegations.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message to Nvidia staff on Sunday. "I am deeply sorry."
Rumors of an affair between Huang and Powell have circulated for years, in part because Powell lacks a background in health or science, according to a former employee who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter.
Nvidia's stock is down 7% this week and is on pace for its sixth straight weekly slide, reflecting broad concern on the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The AI infrastructure trade was hit particularly hard last week after the midterm elections, as Democrats won sweeping majorities in both houses of Congress, and dozens of ballot measures past that could make building data centers more difficult.
Huang has become synonymous with the AI industry, and he is often referred to by his first name ,"Jensen," by customers and rivals. Nvidia has been one of the primary beneficiaries of the AI boom since its chips are used to train models and run large AI workloads.
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny and Kif Leswing contributed to this report

articles.content_orig:
Stocks were higher Wednesday, boosted by sharp gains in CoreWeave and a rebound in Nvidia following back-to-back losing sessions for the chipmaker.
The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.60% to end at 25,466.19, while the S&P 500 advanced 1.31% to 7,619.38. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 254.60 points, or 0.49%, and closed at 52,486.49.
Neocloud stock CoreWeave rallied nearly 25% after reporting third-quarter revenue that beat analyst expectations. CoreWeave also lifted operating income and revenue guidance for 2026.
Nvidia, meanwhile, climbed 2.9% after dropping nearly 10% to start the week when CEO Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The pullback in Nvidia weighed on the broader market Tuesday, with the major averages ending the session lower.
Artificial intelligence lab Anthropic on Tuesday said in an updated Securities and Exchange Commission filing that it will offer 825 million shares in an initial public offering planned for next week that could value the five-year-old company at as much as $1.4 trillion.
"The sentiment bump coming from CoreWeave results and Anthropic IPO demand is helping the broader ecosystem," Ross Mayfield, an investment strategist at Baird Private Wealth Management, told CNBC. "Markets are continuing to unwind last week's overshoot to the downside with cleaner positioning now a tailwind and an attractive near-term valuation/earnings story in a lot of the AI stocks."
Equities fell on Tuesday after stronger-than-expected October inflation data renewed expectations that the Federal Reserve will again raise interest rates at its final policy meeting of the year in December. The consumer price index increased by 0.4% month over month in October , topping economists' estimates.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee sounded the alarm over that latest CPI figure.
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said Tuesday in an interview with "PBS NewsHour ."
Expectations for a quarter-point rate increase next month rose to about 90% following the Dept. of Labor release, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
"Despite some technical uncertainty, higher than desired levels of inflation should keep the Fed in a stance of dissatisfaction with the degree of progress on inflation remaining lackluster, so hiking the Fed Funds policy rate in December is our and the market's base case," wrote Rick Rieder, CIO of global fixed income at BlackRock. "The question now is more of one of the extent of the hike."
Comments from Fed Governor Christopher Waller at a Bank of England conference in London Tuesday also led traders to price in a greater chance of a quarter-point move.
The U.S. bond market was closed on Wednesday for Veterans Day.
U.S. stocks finished Wednesday's session in positive territory.
The S&P 500 jumped 1.31% to end the day at 7,619.38, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.6% to close at 25,466.19. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 254.60 points, or 0.49%, to finish at 52,486.49.
Stocks can continue to climb on a broad basis, even if technology names lost ground, according to Goldman Sachs.
"One of the questions that has been permeating investor conversations this year is 'can the market go up if Tech goes down,'" a Goldman Sachs analyst wrote in a recent note to clients.  "While it's tempting to just say 'no,' November market price action provides a microcosm of the trade that suggests the answer may be 'yes.'"
The analyst noted that energy is the only sector in November that has underperformed info tech in the S&P 500 . Nevertheless, the broad-market index is still up 0.6% month to date.
The observation comes after the Nasdaq Composite slipped earlier this week, as losses in Nvidia led tech stocks lower.
Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, told CNBC's The Exchange on Wednesday that he doesn't think the market has hit the top of the AI trade, although he said he didn't know whether bear market conditions had materialized.
"I don't think it's the top for one simple reason: Agentic AI is very, very new," he said, touting the mass appeal of Meta's consumer AI product, Muse.
Asked about the possibility of a pullback in overall capex and equipment spending during the AI buildout, Niles said that such a scenario could present a problem for the market.
"If you're starting to pull back, then you've got an issue because now you're dealing with the other side of this, and in fact, it is March of 2000," he said, comparing the contingency he described to the popping of the dot-com bubble.
Even if the market enters a bear market, Niles said, it doesn't really matter for the way that he invests because investors can still play for strong positive rallies even as the overall trajectory is in decline.
Apple is set to close at another all-time high on Wednesday, two days after doing the same thing on Monday, when it finished the day at $350.69.
So far, the all-time intraday high of $355.38 reached last Thursday Nov. 5 remains unsurpassed.
Apple, the largest company in the U.S. with a market capitalization of some $5.1 trillion, has so far reached three all-time closing highs in November alone. The iPhone maker has soared 30.5% so far in 2026, nearly three times the 11.6% gain in the S&P 500.
Mortgage rates fell for four straight weeks, but that ended Tuesday, after a monthly inflation report came in hotter than expected. The average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage rose 12 basis points from Monday to 7.30%, according to Mortgage News Daily. It was the largest one-day jump in more than a month.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "borderline disturbing."
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said in an interview with the PBS NewsHour Tuesday.
"We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Goolsbee said. "We're going to have to deal with that."
The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Tuesday morning release. That was higher than economists had predicted, and the third straight month of outsized price increases.
CoreWeave shares jumped 20% Wednesday after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year.
"Demand for the infrastructure is and remains overwhelming." CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Wednesday.
"I think I said that we are 10x oversubscribed to the existing capacity that we have left in 2027, and we are multiples ... oversubscribed on the capacity we have out in 2028," he said.
Berkshire Hathaway 's "Buffett premium" is evaporating, according to CFRA, citing "eroding fundamentals" and uncertainty around the "significant management transition."
In a Tuesday note, analyst Catherine Seifert highlighted insurance as a "weak spot" in during the firm's third quarter, which reported a decline in operating earnings .
She also mentioned shares of Berkshire "merit caution in the near term." At current levels, the stock trades at about 25 times CFRA's 2026 operating earnings per share, above their three-year average forward multiple of 23 times.
Warren Buffett announced his retirement as CEO at the end of 2025. He remains the chairman emeritus and a Board Director at the firm.
Current CEO Greg Abel, a CPA and the former CEO of MidAmerican Energy, brings "strong operational skills" to this role. Although, he still has big shoes to fill.
Still, Seifert highlighted bright spots, including Berkshire's balance sheet which continues to reflect "solid financial strength" as well as buybacks.
In Q3, the conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock.
Analysts at JPMorgan upgraded Republic Services to overweight from neutral, raising its price target to $295, implying nearly 19% upside from Tuesday's close.

articles.content_orig:
U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.
John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.
Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody.
Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant said John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed.
CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the company and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP.
AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have said is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized.
On its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The company said it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand.
But the affidavit said that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States …."
The affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.
The company's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court."
The company has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC.
And in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the company, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor.
In an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris said last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally.
The central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients.
But an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs."
In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV.
In a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson said the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk."
CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.
— CNBC's Paige Tortorelli and Melissa Lee contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: US auto workers union urges Congress to keep its eye on Chinese automakers
articles.title_zh: US auto workers union urges Congress to keep its eye on Chinese automakers
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON, Nov 11 (Reuters) – The United Auto Workers union urged top US lawmakers to keep the House China Select Committee in place when Democrats take over, citing concerns about ​Chinese automakers, according to a letter seen by Reuters on ‌Wednesday.
“From global overcapacity in electric vehicles, Chinese ownership of Western automakers, and continued offshoring to China, we urgently need Congress’s focused attention on these issues and their rapidly emerging downstream effects,” the UAW wrote House Speaker Mike Johnson and Democratic Leader ‌Hakeem ​Jeffries. “Autoworkers cannot afford any lapse in Congress’s ⁠attention on this issue.”
Jeffries said ⁠this week he would meet with Democratic leaders on the future of the House China select committee.
The House select committee under Republican Representative John Moolenaar has investigated a number of China-related issues, including ​Ford’s partnership with Chinese battery company CATL and an abandoned plan of a subsidiary of Chinese battery company Gotion to build a $2.4 ⁠billion plant in Michigan to produce battery ⁠materials.
Moolenaar said this week the committee work should continue ​next year. “The challenges we face as a nation are only becoming more ​urgent given the high-stakes technology competition in AI and (China’s) growing coercion ‌targeting America’s allies and partners,” he said.
Congress has yet to pass legislation to make permanent a ban on Chinese autos. Senator Bernie Moreno, a Republican co-author of the bill, told Reuters on Tuesday he was ⁠getting “really, really close” to a deal and hoping for a Senate vote as early as next week.
“Congress must ensure that China and its practices do ⁠not gain a foothold ‌in the US market,” the UAW letter said.
A ⁠group representing General Motors, Toyota, Volkswagen and other major ​automakers ‌is lobbying Congress to complete work on the Chinese ​auto ban ⁠this year.
A regulation imposed by former President Joe Biden in early 2025 effectively banned Chinese automakers from selling or building passenger vehicles in the US because they could send sensitive driver data to China. Washington also maintains more than 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.
(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing ​by David Gregorio)

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq gains more than 1% as CoreWeave spike revitalizes AI trade
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq gains more than 1% as CoreWeave spike revitalizes AI trade
articles.content_orig:
Stocks were higher Wednesday, boosted by sharp gains in CoreWeave and a rebound in Nvidia following back-to-back losing sessions for the chipmaker.
The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.60% to end at 25,466.19, while the S&P 500 advanced 1.31% to 7,619.38. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 254.60 points, or 0.49%, and closed at 52,486.49.
Neocloud stock CoreWeave rallied nearly 25% after reporting third-quarter revenue that beat analyst expectations. CoreWeave also lifted operating income and revenue guidance for 2026.
Nvidia, meanwhile, climbed 2.9% after dropping nearly 10% to start the week when CEO Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The pullback in Nvidia weighed on the broader market Tuesday, with the major averages ending the session lower.
Artificial intelligence lab Anthropic on Tuesday said in an updated Securities and Exchange Commission filing that it will offer 825 million shares in an initial public offering planned for next week that could value the five-year-old company at as much as $1.4 trillion.
"The sentiment bump coming from CoreWeave results and Anthropic IPO demand is helping the broader ecosystem," Ross Mayfield, an investment strategist at Baird Private Wealth Management, told CNBC. "Markets are continuing to unwind last week's overshoot to the downside with cleaner positioning now a tailwind and an attractive near-term valuation/earnings story in a lot of the AI stocks."
Equities fell on Tuesday after stronger-than-expected October inflation data renewed expectations that the Federal Reserve will again raise interest rates at its final policy meeting of the year in December. The consumer price index increased by 0.4% month over month in October , topping economists' estimates.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee sounded the alarm over that latest CPI figure.
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said Tuesday in an interview with "PBS NewsHour ."
Expectations for a quarter-point rate increase next month rose to about 90% following the Dept. of Labor release, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
"Despite some technical uncertainty, higher than desired levels of inflation should keep the Fed in a stance of dissatisfaction with the degree of progress on inflation remaining lackluster, so hiking the Fed Funds policy rate in December is our and the market's base case," wrote Rick Rieder, CIO of global fixed income at BlackRock. "The question now is more of one of the extent of the hike."
Comments from Fed Governor Christopher Waller at a Bank of England conference in London Tuesday also led traders to price in a greater chance of a quarter-point move.
The U.S. bond market was closed on Wednesday for Veterans Day.
U.S. stocks finished Wednesday's session in positive territory.
The S&P 500 jumped 1.31% to end the day at 7,619.38, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.6% to close at 25,466.19. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 254.60 points, or 0.49%, to finish at 52,486.49.
Stocks can continue to climb on a broad basis, even if technology names lost ground, according to Goldman Sachs.
"One of the questions that has been permeating investor conversations this year is 'can the market go up if Tech goes down,'" a Goldman Sachs analyst wrote in a recent note to clients.  "While it's tempting to just say 'no,' November market price action provides a microcosm of the trade that suggests the answer may be 'yes.'"
The analyst noted that energy is the only sector in November that has underperformed info tech in the S&P 500 . Nevertheless, the broad-market index is still up 0.6% month to date.
The observation comes after the Nasdaq Composite slipped earlier this week, as losses in Nvidia led tech stocks lower.
Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, told CNBC's The Exchange on Wednesday that he doesn't think the market has hit the top of the AI trade, although he said he didn't know whether bear market conditions had materialized.
"I don't think it's the top for one simple reason: Agentic AI is very, very new," he said, touting the mass appeal of Meta's consumer AI product, Muse.
Asked about the possibility of a pullback in overall capex and equipment spending during the AI buildout, Niles said that such a scenario could present a problem for the market.
"If you're starting to pull back, then you've got an issue because now you're dealing with the other side of this, and in fact, it is March of 2000," he said, comparing the contingency he described to the popping of the dot-com bubble.
Even if the market enters a bear market, Niles said, it doesn't really matter for the way that he invests because investors can still play for strong positive rallies even as the overall trajectory is in decline.
Apple is set to close at another all-time high on Wednesday, two days after doing the same thing on Monday, when it finished the day at $350.69.
So far, the all-time intraday high of $355.38 reached last Thursday Nov. 5 remains unsurpassed.
Apple, the largest company in the U.S. with a market capitalization of some $5.1 trillion, has so far reached three all-time closing highs in November alone. The iPhone maker has soared 30.5% so far in 2026, nearly three times the 11.6% gain in the S&P 500.
Mortgage rates fell for four straight weeks, but that ended Tuesday, after a monthly inflation report came in hotter than expected. The average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage rose 12 basis points from Monday to 7.30%, according to Mortgage News Daily. It was the largest one-day jump in more than a month.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "borderline disturbing."
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said in an interview with the PBS NewsHour Tuesday.
"We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Goolsbee said. "We're going to have to deal with that."
The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Tuesday morning release. That was higher than economists had predicted, and the third straight month of outsized price increases.
CoreWeave shares jumped 20% Wednesday after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year.
"Demand for the infrastructure is and remains overwhelming." CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Wednesday.
"I think I said that we are 10x oversubscribed to the existing capacity that we have left in 2027, and we are multiples ... oversubscribed on the capacity we have out in 2028," he said.
Berkshire Hathaway 's "Buffett premium" is evaporating, according to CFRA, citing "eroding fundamentals" and uncertainty around the "significant management transition."
In a Tuesday note, analyst Catherine Seifert highlighted insurance as a "weak spot" in during the firm's third quarter, which reported a decline in operating earnings .
She also mentioned shares of Berkshire "merit caution in the near term." At current levels, the stock trades at about 25 times CFRA's 2026 operating earnings per share, above their three-year average forward multiple of 23 times.
Warren Buffett announced his retirement as CEO at the end of 2025. He remains the chairman emeritus and a Board Director at the firm.
Current CEO Greg Abel, a CPA and the former CEO of MidAmerican Energy, brings "strong operational skills" to this role. Although, he still has big shoes to fill.
Still, Seifert highlighted bright spots, including Berkshire's balance sheet which continues to reflect "solid financial strength" as well as buybacks.
In Q3, the conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock.
Analysts at JPMorgan upgraded Republic Services to overweight from neutral, raising its price target to $295, implying nearly 19% upside from Tuesday's close.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Dividends are a nice little perk of being a shareholder, along with holding a stake in a company that you believe in, which will hopefully increase in value over time.
Depending on the stock and how much you own, the payouts can be quite decent, even wading into double-digit percentage territory for some high-yield (though usually volatile) equities. But even when returns are relatively meager, the extra cash can be enough to completely offset certain everyday costs — like, say, a Costco membership.

In the case of Costco Wholesale Corp. [NASDAQ: COST] stock, the quarterly dividend and associated stock owner benefits can actually end up covering your entire annual enrollment fee, making it somewhat of a "hack" for loyal shoppers.
On Nov. 10, the beloved American warehouse brand announced that a special cash dividend , amounting to $30 per share, will be paid out to all investors on December 4, 2026. Considering that a Personal or Business Costco card is $65 a year , that means just three shares could completely finance your dues for the year.
However, it should be noted that the capital return is only available to those who serve as shareholders of record by the end of day on Nov. 24, 2026. And per the IRS, the shares must be held for more than 60 days for the dividend to be considered qualified . This will affect how the dividend is taxed if shares are held in a taxable brokerage account (qualified dividends are taxed at long-term capital gains rates, while regular dividends are taxed at a typical income tax rate).

This new disbursement comes on top of the fact that, theoretically, the amount customers save on their shopping hauls should more than cancel out the fee for said membership. The retail titan also periodically holds promotions that include statement credits or vouchers with sign-up, and tends to offer special cash dividends to investors every few years , making it even more worth it.
Costco continues to inspire membership growth and consumer loyalty through its exclusive in-house label — which also helps safeguard the company against tariffs and inflation — alongside its rock-bottom prices (due to narrow product markups ) and unique bulk offerings. Most of its profit comes from membership payments, while sales pay for its svelte operations and resulting low overhead costs.
In its release about the cash dividend, the Costco board also verified a common-stock repurchase program of up to $4 billion to replace the one expiring at the start of January 2027. It will run until November 2030.
Other "hacks" that dividend recipients have been known to take advantage of include free meals at annual meetings; one man went viral on TikTok for showcasing the bougie shareholder dinner he was able to attend for owning just one $18 share in a luxury property developer.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO Is ‘Jenga Block’ Holding Up Next Leg of AI Trade
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO Is ‘Jenga Block’ Holding Up Next Leg of AI Trade
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, according to an updated filing on Tuesday, bringing the 5-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut.
The company is planning to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is targeting retail allocation of about 20%, the people said, a much higher percentage than the typical initial public offering, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors.
At the high end of the range, Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds through the IPO. The company could end up being worth up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, rising from the $965 billion valuation it announced as part of a funding round in May.
Anthropic said it has entered into an agreement with Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. to purchase $26 billion of the company's Class N common stock in a private placement at a price per share equal to the IPO price. The shares sold in the private placement will not be registered in the offering and will not be subject to lock-up agreements with the underwriters, the company said.
As Anthropic executives get set to pitch the offering to investors, they have to contend with a tumultuous political environment , following last week's midterm elections that included a Democratic sweep in Congress and the passage of numerous statewide ballot measures that could slow the AI buildout. They're also facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade on concern that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases.
CNBC reported last week that some Anthropic investors were bracing for a lower valuation than had previously been expected. While Anthropic had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation until recently, shareholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch."
Should Anthropic reach the Nasdaq this month as planned, under the ticker symbol "ANT," the debut would come roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. Elon Musk's reusable rocket and AI company has a market cap of just under $2 trillion, around its valuation at the time of the IPO.
Institutional demand for Anthropic is even stronger than it was for SpaceX at this point in the process, the people said. The company's book is already covered at the $70 to $78 per share range on an allocable basis, they said.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the AI lab in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and the company primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
On Monday, Anthropic introduced two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the first time the company has released so-called frontier models since Amodei called to slow down the pace of AI development in September . Anthropic said that the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release.
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic said in its amended filing Tuesday that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.
"Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. We hope you will share our ambition to see it though."
