articles.title_orig: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
articles.title_zh: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
articles.content_orig:
Joe is based in Brussels, where he focuses on European politics and defence. He has covered the Ukraine war and its peace negotiations and reported on US elections from Washington DC
Britain and France should immediately deploy troops to Ukraine, a former head of Nato has said.
Anders Fogh Rasmussen accused Europe’s two nuclear powers of presiding over a “coalition of the waiting” while the Kremlin dragged out peace talks.
“For some months, France and the UK have tried to establish a coalition of the willing, but it’s more now a coalition of the waiting,” the 73-year-old former Danish prime minister told The Telegraph from his office in Brussels.
“We should transform that into a ‘coalition of the doing’ by deploying troops… you could not wait for a peace deal but actually push for peace by telling Putin ‘you cannot deter us, and we will help the Ukrainians defend against attacks against their critical infrastructure’.”
Mr Rasmussen’s call for action came during US-led negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine and Russia, which focused on security guarantees and preventing a future war.
European officials were kept out of the room after Moscow objected to their involvement in the two-day talks, which Ukraine described on Wednesday as “one of the toughest” negotiations yet.
Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, said after the talks: “We have no idea what the Europeans are doing here, this is a trilateral meeting. They can hang out in the lobby if they want.”
Mr Rasmussen, who was Nato’s secretary-general between 2009 and 2014, believes that Europe must show Vladimir Putin that it is serious in its support for Ukraine, even as it continues to be denied a seat at the table.
He has devised a five-point strategy to stop the war and prevent Europe from “sleepwalking into a permanent war on the Continent”.
He called on Germany, Spain and Greece to empty their stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to help Kyiv protect itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks, and suggested Nato extends its integrated air and missile defence systems over western Ukraine to bolster defences.
On top of this, Mr Rasmussen said the EU should confiscate more than €200bn (£175bn) in frozen Russian assets and use them to top up Kyiv’s defence budget. The “Coalition of the Willing” should be overhauled to include only countries willing to go to war with Russia should it attack Ukraine after any ceasefire is negotiated, he added.
“President Trump has chosen Moscow and sided with Vladimir Putin,” Mr Rasmussen said. “So in Europe, we have a particular responsibility for helping Ukraine, and that’s why I call on European leaders to wake up.”
He added: “It’s clear that the Russians do not want peace. Putin has no incentives to engage in the peace negotiations as long as he believes he can succeed on the battlefield.
“So, we need to change his calculus, we need to put more pressure on Russia.”
His plan would involve French and British troops as a “reassurance force” to protect Ukraine’s population centres.
It would also free up more Ukrainian resources to commit to the front line with Russia.
Mr Rasmussen insisted that such a deployment would be in line with international rules as long as it was requested by Kyiv.
However, Mr Rasmussen’s ideas are likely to be controversial amongst Europe’s Nato allies.
Numerous countries have said they would not actively shoot down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory for fear of becoming a genuine party to the conflict.
Belgium has repeatedly blocked EU discussions about using a tranche of frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine’s defence.
While Germany has recently warned that it cannot donate any more Patriot interceptor missiles because it doesn’t have the stockpiles to defend its own country.
“Maybe Poland is in a different situation, but Germany, I don’t understand why they cannot deliver those Patriot systems. Deliver them now; they are needed right now in Ukraine… Germany is not threatened now,” Mr Rasmussen said.
The former Nato chief, who was involved in talks with Russia when it first invaded Ukraine’s Crimea peninsula in 2014, said the Continent was right to reopen communication channels with Moscow.
But he warned against linking discussions on a ceasefire in Ukraine to negotiations over a future European security architecture, arguing that Putin would seek to exploit the talks to restrict the military capabilities of both Kyiv and the alliance.
That said, Mr Rasmussen believes Nato could ultimately offer Russia security guarantees, given that its allies have no plans to attack Moscow.
“Why not? It wouldn’t cost anything to give such a security guarantee,” he concluded.

articles.title_orig: Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?
articles.title_zh: Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?
articles.content_orig:
AUSTIN, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 26: A gas pump is seen in a vehicle on November 26, 2025 in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell/Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Drivers are starting to see some relief from high fuel prices. For the first time in months, the average price of a gallon of gasoline has dipped below $4, according to AAA .
The price crossed below the $4 threshold on Tuesday, and is currently down to a national average of $3.94 for a gallon of regular. Prices have dipped about 40 cents over the past month, with much of that decline happening in the past two weeks.
"Many will assume the election had something to do with it, but that's a myth," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in his industry newsletter .
Instead, he continued, gasoline prices are dropping for a more banal reason: "For now, it's the seasonal shift, not politics, driving the relief at the pump."
Gas prices often ease in the fall.
One reason: It's no longer summer, which is the peak season for gas. (Fewer people drive in colder weather, AAA points out .) With less demand, there's a touch more gas on the market.
Refineries also finish their annual maintenance by late fall. So that adds a bit more gas to go around.
And the blend of gasoline that's on the market gets cheaper.
Refineries make two types of gasoline every year: summer and winter blends. The summer blend produces less smog, because it evaporates less quickly in the heat; the winter blend helps engines start up in freezing weather, and uses a bit more butane, which helps lower its cost.
(Normally, the switch happens around September 15. This year, the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Energy said the switch would happen on September 1, citing gasoline prices that have been driven up by the war in Iran.)
But none of those are the biggest reason why gas prices are falling, says Jorge León, head of geopolitics at the research group Rystad Energy. The main driver is the falling price of Brent crude oil, which is now down to about $90 a barrel, and which is what refineries need to make gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
That price is falling because there's a bit more oil coming out of the Middle East via pipelines, and because market traders have rejoiced at the intensifying diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran.
That progress could easily be reversed if the war escalates, León wrote in an email to NPR. "President Trump may see further military action as a way to regain negotiating leverage before Democrats take control of Congress in January. If we see renewed escalation, much of last week's oil price decline could quickly reverse," he wrote. The same would be true for gas prices.
Congressional Democrats have expressed their support for ending the war in Iran. While they have limited power to do that, they do control the power of the purse, and can withhold additional war funding or hold back confirmations of key officials.
For now, if the price of Brent crude keeps falling, so could prices at the pump. "However, this does not mean a complete 'normalization,' a return to the price levels we had before this conflict started," Jaime Brito, executive director of refining and oil markets for Dow Jones Energy, wrote in an email to NPR.
To get back to pre-Iran war gas prices, the whole oil supply chain would have to recover. Ships that have been running long alternative routes to avoid the Strait of Hormuz would have to return to their points of origin, then resume their normal routes, taking crude oil to refineries. Those refineries would have to pump out enough fuel to alleviate global demand — and depleted stockpiles. The whole process could take months after a lasting peace deal.
"Coming back to those levels will require a return to normal crude production, shipping and refining of the entire global supply chain," Brito continued.
And while $4 a gallon may seem like a bargain these days, in an update on its website, AAA said that gasoline prices are still the highest they've ever been at this time of year.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi bring progress on prisoners but not on peace
articles.title_zh: Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi bring progress on prisoners but not on peace
articles.content_orig:
US envoys to visit Moscow and Dublin on Thursday for talks with Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy respectively
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to the “largest prisoner exchange” of the war at their first US-brokered talks since February but made little progress towards a broader peace agreement.
Both sides sent senior delegations to the two-day talks, led by Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, in an effort to find a solution to end the nearly-five-year war.
David Arakhamia, a senior member of Ukraine’s delegation, said the Russian team had arrived with “very, very strict directives”, making it difficult to narrow differences. But he said there had been “really big progress” on security guarantees for Ukraine after the war. “I think we have good momentum to bring about a solution before the new year,” Arakhamia said.
Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, also struck an upbeat tone, saying he could see a path to an agreement. “These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” he said. “But we see all the different ingredients to make a deal. We just have to figure out how to refine those ingredients, organise them and create the right structure and pathway.”
Kushner said the planned exchange, expected to involve more than 1,000 prisoners from each side, would “reunite families, build trust and create momentum towards peace”.
The US envoys are due to travel to Moscow on Thursday to discuss the Abu Dhabi talks with Vladimir Putin, before heading to Dublin, where they are expected to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy and a group of European partners.
“In close coordination with Ukraine and our European partners, we have aligned on proposals we will discuss with President Putin in Moscow tomorrow, followed by consultations with President Zelenskyy,” Kushner said.
But despite the optimism, Kushner also said the two sides had yet to resolve their territorial dispute.
Russia’s territorial demands have shifted over time, but Moscow has made clear it wants control of all the Donbas, including areas still held by Kyiv, as well as the parts of two southern regions it does not yet occupy.
Vladimir Medinsky, the hardline Russian official who led Moscow’s delegation, said that “every inch of our land will be returned to Russia, one way or another,” in a sign that Moscow was unwilling to soften its territorial demands. Russia would be satisfied with the negotiations only “when there is peace on its terms”, he added.
He also said the main task was to create a new security system in Europe that would become “a new Yalta and Potsdam”.
Medinsky said Europe’s post-second world war security system was failing, with Ukraine merely the place where its wider problems had erupted. “Essentially, the whole body is sick, and Ukraine was just a cyst that burst. The whole body must be cured. A Band-Aid won’t be enough,” Medinsky said.
His focus on Europe’s wider security order is likely to heighten concern among European leaders that Washington and Moscow could reach a broader agreement on the continent’s security, potentially limiting Nato’s military presence in eastern Europe. Russia appears to be seeking to revive demands it presented to Nato in 2021, including a halt to further enlargement that would rule out Ukraine’s membership, restrictions on Nato forces and weapons in European countries that joined after 1997, and limits on missile deployments.
That ultimatum was dismissed as a non-starter by the west and, weeks later, Russia invaded Ukraine .
Concerned that Europe’s security future could be discussed over their heads, European governments sent envoys to Abu Dhabi to try to influence the talks, although they are not believed to have taken part directly.
Medinsky dismissed their presence, saying that if they had come “as tourists”, they could talk in the hotel lobby, and that Russia would consider proposals only if they had “something specific” to offer.
European leaders have increasingly discussed the need for a direct channel to Putin , but no clear candidate has emerged. The leaders of Norway and Finland have recently spoken to the Russian president, while Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said on Wednesday that he was open to doing so.
Kushner, meanwhile, said Europe should choose a single representative to speak on its behalf. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said.
He stressed that one of the aims of his trip to Moscow was to “see if we can get Europeans added” to future talks. “The issues that were covered in these discussions were really postwar security,” he said. “How do we make sure that once this war ends, it doesn’t start again?”
Russian officials have long opposed European participation, arguing that countries supplying weapons to Kyiv cannot act as impartial mediators. Medinsky said Russia would speak to European countries only “when their conscience awakens” and they stop supplying Ukraine with weapons.
As diplomatic efforts continued, both sides kept up their attacks. Russia launched drones at Kyiv and other regions during the day, while Ukraine struck the Ust-Luga port on Russia’s Baltic coast overnight. The port, in the Leningrad region, is a major route for Russian energy exports and was still burning on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
articles.title_zh: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
articles.content_orig:
United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.
Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.
To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.
"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.
United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.
"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."
Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.
United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."
"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.
Kris  Van Cleave contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: For Families of Those Who Died in the Iran War, a Veterans Day of Profound Loss
articles.title_zh: For Families of Those Who Died in the Iran War, a Veterans Day of Profound Loss
articles.content_orig:
This Armistice Day, CEO of OpenUK Amanda Brock argues that it is more important to regulate behaviour than technology.
This week marked Armistice Day, 11th November, when we wear poppies to commemorate the dead of the First and Second World Wars. We remember that they made the ultimate sacrifice for our freedom. Last Sunday, I was home in Crieff and saw the Remembrance parade. Wreaths were laid, as they were across the country, but it was the horses accompanying the procession that particularly stayed with me.
Over the summer, I saw War Horse at the National Theatre. It's a deeply moving story of a young man who enlists underage to find his beloved horse, Joey, after the horse is sold to the cavalry in the First World War. The contrast between the human relationships at the heart of the story and the increasingly technical and devastating reality of war was poignant. When British foot soldiers advanced at the Somme in July 1916, they faced machine-gun fire. By September, the British had introduced tanks into battle for the first time, in part to overcome the defences that had inflicted such heavy losses on them.
As told in the play, that began the technologisation of war. This process is one that has evolved over 100 years. Perhaps realistically it dates back to munitions and ammunition being developed. The turning point for the British forces as told in the play, what tipped the battle of the Somme, was the tank being rolled out by the British military, seeing the evolution of technology to fight technology.
A century later, warfare is still fought, but less through boots on the ground and increasingly shaped by technology, from drones and cyberattacks to AI-enabled intelligence and autonomous systems.
Ukraine has demonstrated how drones can change the balance of military power. Meanwhile, planes undertake emergency landings across Europe and fridges in the food supply chain are turned off – potentially by nation states . This disruption reminds us that the consequences of modern technological threats extend well beyond the battlefield.
In considering AI policy and regulation, we need to recognise the environment in which these technologies operate. Innovation can create both enormous opportunities and significant risks. The challenge is how to address those risks without unnecessarily restricting the technologies themselves.
Nick Clegg, now at Hiro Capital, has spoken this week about the disconnect between Big Tech, politics, and the willingness of these companies to express political opinion.
The same is true in reverse. A Baroness commented to me that she was shocked by how political - with a small p - tech is. That’s because the decisions on a word in a regulation is the difference between a loss and a billion-dollar revenue stream.
Neither sufficiently understands the other's world to make decisions that impact on the other. Yet decisions about technology increasingly shape almost every aspect of our lives and the delivery of our basic services. Hardly surprising when every aspect of our daily lives is reliant on technology today.
There is only one certainty in this digital world: we can only go forward, not back.
Of course, there’s much debate as to whether we regulate the underlying technology or how it is used. A bread knife can slice a loaf or be used as a weapon. We don't prohibit bread knives because they can cause harm; instead, we regulate harmful behaviour. The same distinction matters when considering general purpose technologies like AI. Generally we regulate use cases, and attempts to regulate coding per se would not be wise. We look to greater regulation in particular areas - regulated sectors - and that is appropriate.
The assumption that open source is inherently less secure persists, despite the evidence that security depends on far more than whether innovation is open or closed. Both forms have different challenges. Frankly, all technology has security challenges, and we need to consider what those are and how they are securely managed for a particular use case.
The Ukranians built drones on Arduino to use them in large-scale attacks. We see much of today’s warfare in Ukraine and in Iran being driven by technology. Ukraine's use of open source technologies in drone development illustrates how innovation can be adapted to meet urgent military needs. But the use of open technologies in warfare does not make the openness itself the problem. We need to distinguish between the technology, the people developing it and the purposes for which it is deployed.
What matters is how technology is developed, maintained, and deployed. Openness can support scrutiny that enables trust, but it is not a substitute for good security practice. The last conversation I had with Sir Alex Younger, former head of MI6, ended with him saying, with a smile, “May the open source be with you.” That followed a long discussion on why open source is not detrimental to security.
Regulators are challenged by complex technologies that evolve quickly. Those who understand the technologies are generally nowhere near the regulatory process.
Trust in AI remains a challenge in the West, and sensible regulation and policy has an important role to play in building it.
We must focus on addressing demonstrable risks, ensuring accountability and understanding how technologies are used, rather than treating innovation or openness as threats in themselves. To do this we need more of the right people in the room, bringing real technical understanding and building assurance.
In this world of geopolitical uncertainty good technological understanding in our policy has never mattered more.

articles.title_orig: Protesters Throw Projectiles at Biden During Dublin Trip
articles.title_zh: Protesters Throw Projectiles at Biden During Dublin Trip
articles.content_orig:
Three men have been arrested after protesters pelted former President Joe Biden with objects outside a university in Dublin, police in Ireland said Wednesday.
Videos showed protesters, some waving Palestinian flags, chanting “Blood on your hands” and scuffling with police officers outside Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday, as he attended a ceremony honoring his son Hunter Biden, alongside former first lady Jill Biden . White liquid, believed to be milk, could also be seen flying through the air toward the group.
Hunter Biden was being honored by its traditional Hist debating society , which dates back to 1770. Previous recipients of the gold medal for outstanding contribution to public discourse include Irish musician Bob Geldof, South African Bishop Desmond Tutu , WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange and the late Sen. Ted Kennedy.
During his acceptance speech, Hunter Biden discussed his addictions, family life and being in the public eye. “We are living in an age of bullies,” he said , adding that he had learned this from “my own scars.”
Shortly after the ceremony, a “protest took place in Trinity’s Front Square,” Catherine O’Mahony, a spokesperson for the college, said in a statement to NBC News on Wednesday.
She said “the protest escalated while the Bidens were leaving,” and Irish police, known as the Gardaí, arrived at the scene. “The Biden family left without incident. The protest dispersed soon after,” she added.
Police said in a statement Wednesday that three men were arrested “in relation to a public order incident” at Trinity College Dublin. One man in his 50s “has since been charged and is due to appear before Court. The two other males have been released without charge.” The statement did not say what the man had been charged with.
Representatives for the elder Biden did not immediately reply to a request for comment about the incident.
Ireland has long had a historical solidarity with the Palestinian cause, with pro-Palestinian flags, murals and graffiti a common sight around the country.
Many in the country compare the current situation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank with Ireland’s experience of British colonial rule and struggle for self-determination. Ireland was also the recent venue for American rapper Macklemore’s sold-out “Free Palestine Tour,” which opened in Dublin last month.
The Bidens, who have Irish heritage, also met with Ireland’s Taoiseach, or prime minister, Micheál Martin.
“We reflected on his strong Irish roots and previous visits, appreciating his lifelong support for Ireland,” Martin said on X of his meeting with the former president.
During a 2023 visit to the country while he was president, Biden told the Irish Parliament in an emotional address that he was “home.”
Biden’s great-great-grandfather Owen Finnegan left the Irish county of Louth for the United States in 1849, and he also has relatives from another side of his family in County Mayo, on Ireland’s west coast.
Earlier this week, Biden, 83, signaled he was scaling back public tours to promote his upcoming memoir “Promise Me, America,” as he continues his treatment for cancer.
“Some days are better than others,” Biden wrote Sunday in a lengthy post on X . “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”
Biden announced that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer months after he left office in January 2025 and has since undertaken courses of radiation therapy and hormone treatment.
He said his doctors were “encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment” and thanked the public for its prayers and well-wishes.
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.

articles.title_orig: iCloud+ has new perk in iOS 27 if you pay for more storage
articles.title_zh: iCloud+ has new perk in iOS 27 if you pay for more storage
articles.content_orig:
The tentpole feature of iCloud+ is cloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding the service to include other perks too. And in iOS 27, iCloud+ has a new benefit for high-storage tiers: AI features for HomeKit cameras.
With iOS 27, iCloud+ has added a new perk if you pay for more storage: Apple Intelligence features for compatible Home cameras. Per Apple’s website :
With Apple Intelligence in the Home app, you can automatically generate video descriptions for recorded clips from compatible Home cameras. You can then search your recordings using natural language
These AI-generated video descriptions provide a convenient summary of what’s happening in your home, let you browse important clips at a glance, and search the camera’s recent history of recordings.
All of this is available with a camera that supports HomeKit Secure Video ( I recommend this Aqara camera for $35 ). But because AI features depend on Private Cloud Compute, Apple only offers them on the following iCloud+ plans:
Apple charges $9.99, $29.99, and $59.99/month for each of these plans, respectively. So most users probably won’t find the monthly cost worth it for AI camera features alone. But if you already need a lot of iCloud storage, now you’ll get these new features thrown in too.
Note: these AI features have additional requirements too . You’ll need a home hub like a HomeView, Apple TV 4K, or HomePod, and your iPhone must support Apple Intelligence.
Have you used iOS 27’s new AI features for Home cameras? How are they working for you? Let us know in the comments.
FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.
Check out 9to5Mac on YouTube for more Apple news:
iCloud is built into every Apple device, so that…
Ryan got his start in journalism as an Editor at MacStories, where he worked for four years covering Apple news, writing app reviews, and more. For two years he co-hosted the Adapt podcast on Relay FM, which focused entirely on the iPad. As a result, it should come as no surprise that his favorite Apple device is the iPad Pro.

articles.title_orig: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
articles.title_zh: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
articles.content_orig:
The United Kingdom has pledged to defend its interests in the Sea Lion project to develop an oilfield near the Falkland Islands, as Argentina has brought a legal challenge before a tribunal over the offshore oil exploration, citing environmental concerns.
Attorney General Ellie Reeves, representing the UK government at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), said billions of pounds that are crucial to the future of the Falkland Islands will be lost if Argentina is successful in getting the project blocked.
The Hamburg-based tribunal is sitting for two days as Argentina seeks a provisional ruling to suspend oil drilling.
Reeves also said Argentina’s objection to the development was rooted in its territorial claims. “The hearing is not about the sovereignty of the Falklands,” the UK prime minister’s official spokesman said on Monday, echoing his country’s position that the islands’ sovereignty is not up for negotiation.
The dispute is the latest in rising tensions between the UK and Argentina over the British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean.
As Vicky Kapogianni, associate professor of international and environmental law at the University of Reading, explained to Al Jazeera: “Sovereignty is the root of the dispute. The oil is the trigger, and the environment is Argentina’s best legal route.”
The Sea Lion development is a UK-Israeli venture to drill for oil in waters administered by the Falklands.
The UK’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum, operator of the Sea Lion oilfield, located about 220km (137 miles) from the islands, are expected to start the project in March 2027, with oil production to begin in 2028.
According to Rockhopper Exploration, the Sea Lion oilfield holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil in place, of which 500 million barrels are recoverable resources.
However, Argentina’s President Javier Milei announced measures to block the development in September and said in a post on X that he had instructed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the country’s legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the UK.
“If in 2 weeks the United Kingdom does not halt the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. THE MALVINAS ARE ARGENTINA’s, and they are defended with facts, not words,” he wrote, using the Argentinian name for the Falkland Islands.
Argentina formally filed a complaint at the tribunal seeking provisional measures against the UK on October 13.
The UK has administered the Falkland Islands since 1833. However, as the territory lies off Argentina’s shores, Buenos Aires claims sovereignty over what it calls Las Malvinas.
Milei has also threatened tougher sanctions on companies involved in the oil exploration project, preventing them from operating in Argentina’s oil and mining sectors.
Milei’s government argues the project violates a United Nations resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions in the islands until their dispute over the territory’s sovereignty is resolved.
But Jorge Emilio Nunez, a reader in legal philosophy at Manchester Metropolitan University, explained that at the core of the proceedings lies the sovereignty question over the Falklands.
“The oil project is the current trigger, but it sits on top of deeper competing claims about title, the self-determination of the islanders, and control of the surrounding maritime spaces and resources,” Nunez told Al Jazeera.
“This is not only a legal dispute. It also involves domestic politics and leaders’ prestige on both sides. When valuable natural resources become commercially viable, the underlying territorial disagreement is reactivated and reframed through legal, environmental and economic arguments. The resource issue does not replace the sovereignty dispute; it intensifies it.”
On Tuesday, Attorney General Reeves told the Law of the Sea Tribunal, which issues legally binding rulings on maritime disputes, that Argentina wanted to “take control of those resources for itself”.
“The provisional measures sought by Argentina would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination,” she said, according to The Guardian.
“The measures sought would have devastating consequences for the Falklands people. They risk losing billions of pounds in money, which is essential for the islands’ economic development.”
But Argentina’s lawyer, Mario Oyarzabal, argued that action was needed to block the project.
“[Argentina] respects the interests of the inhabitants of the islands and their way of life as enshrined in the Argentine constitution … What these British citizens do not have is a right to decide to which state the islands belong,” he said during the hearing, The Guardian reported.
“These resources belong to the Argentine people. Some 46 million of them, including the 1,247 inhabitants born on the islands, whose interests will be duly taken into account,” he added.
In 2013, Falkland islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain with the United Kingdom, despite Argentina’s claims.
University of Reading’s Kapogianni explained that environmental risks are central issues.
“If there is a spill, oil could reach waters of Argentina’s mainland, which nobody disputes are Argentine. So the real questions are: Has the UK properly assessed that risk? Has it shared what it found? Is it ready to plan with Argentina in case of an accident?” Kapogianni told Al Jazeera.
“These are questions that can be decided without deciding who owns the islands. But where Argentina is weaker is when it asks to protect the environment in the waters around the islands themselves, the disputed waters. This is where the problem begins, because it can be assumed that those waters are Argentina’s to protect, which takes us back to the question of sovereignty.
“So yes, in that way, meaning indirectly and through the questions, sovereignty is at the heart of it. But it’s not the question the tribunal can answer. The environment is,” she said.
On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson told the Independent news outlet that the UK was “fully engaged in the UNCLOS [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] process, and we’ll clearly set out our position on Argentina’s request for provisional measures before the Tribunal”.
“We’ll continue to robustly defend our interests and those of the Falkland Islanders,” the spokesperson added.
Last month, Burnham also discussed the bid to block the oil project during a call with United States President Donald Trump .
“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said.
The fraught relationship between the UK and Argentina remains tense and heavily focused on the Falkland Islands.
Milei has capitalised on Trump’s refusal to say whether Washington would support the UK in a future conflict over the Falklands after the US president criticised London for not doing more to support the US during its attacks on Iran.
In September, Milei said the “winds of change” were blowing in Argentina’s favour when it comes to its claims of sovereignty.
“The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said.
At the same time, Argentina is set for an election next year, when the Sea Lion project’s halt could help Milei’s polling position.
To Nunez, the tribunal could have a “modest domestic impact” in the country.
“A visible legal success would allow the government to claim it is actively defending national interests and resources as the Falklands/Malvinas issue carries strong symbolic wei

articles.title_zh: Lawsuit filed over Vanderbilt University cyberattack
articles.content_orig:
According to a 1:01 p.m. CST statement from Vanderbilt University Public Safety, VUIT continues working to fully restore operations across its systems and applications. Campus WiFi, Okta, Outlook, CampusPrint, Brightspace, Zoom, UKG, YES and Slate are available. Box and Microsoft Services, among others, remain disabled.
VUIT is prioritizing restoring business operations such as payroll, payment services, admissions, course registration and public safety. Vanderbilt-issued devices are safe to use. If the community notices any suspicious activity, report any concerns to VUIT.
Vanderbilt is working with law enforcement and government agencies to contain the cybersecurity attack. VUPS will continue to update the university as appropriate.
This is a developing story. The Hustler will continue to provide updates as they become available.
Some students and faculty faced difficulties during registration for classes requiring manual course approval from a professor, per an email from to Communication Studies majors and minors from Isaac West, the director of undergraduate studies. Professors of these courses pre-approve enrollment and typically can manually enroll students into a class section.
Vanderbilt first told The Hustler the night of Nov. 9 that YES was working properly. In a 9 a.m. email the next morning, the university announced that course registration was continuing as planned. Sophomore registration occurred that morning, Nov. 10, at 7 a.m. and today.
West’s email stated that faculty and staff access to certain portions of the registration system in YES remains restricted.
The student ticket claim window for Saturday’s football game against Alabama will open tomorrow at 6 p.m. The window typically opens at 6 p.m. the Monday before a game. The cyberattack prompted Vanderbilt Athletics to postpone the claim window, originally without a rescheduled date.
The university was expected to provide an update today at 10 a.m. CST. As of 11:39 a.m. CST, the university has yet to notify the community of any cybersecurity update.
The Hustler continues to monitor for changes and will update this story as information becomes available.
According to a university statement last night, an update regarding the cybersecurity attack was planned for 10 a.m. CST. As of 10:08 a.m., no update has been sent.
The Hustler conducted a survey on Fizz, an anonymous social app for Vanderbilt students, about Vanderbilt’s response to the cybersecurity attack so far. Of the 2,136 community members surveyed, 79% are either highly dissatisfied or dissatisfied, 6% are either satisfied or highly satisfied, while 15% remain neutral.
Junior Simran Fitzpatrick, Vanderbilt Student Government president, said that these results align with VSG’s sentiment on the incident.
The university is scheduled to release another statement tomorrow at 10 a.m. CST. This story will be updated as more information becomes available.
The FBI field office in Nashville confirmed the agency’s involvement in investigating the cyberattack.
“At this time, we can confirm that the FBI is aware of this cyber incident, and we are assisting our partners,” a representative for the office said.
The office declined to comment further on the ongoing investigation per U.S. Department of Justice policy.
According to a 6:12 p.m. CST statement from Vanderbilt University Public Safety, VUIT continues to contain the cybersecurity attack. VUIT said it may take a few weeks before systems are fully contained. The university is working to restore remaining systems and applications in a timely manner.
Campus Wifi, Okta, Outlook, CampusPrint, Brightspace, Zoom and YES are safe and available for use. According to VUIT, community members should be vigilant about any suspicious activity and report such concerns to VUIT.
The next update to the community is scheduled for tomorrow at 10 a.m. CST.
The Hustler will continue to update this story as more information becomes available.
According to a 9:10 a.m. CST statement from Vanderbilt University Public Safety, Campus WiFi, Okta, Outlook, Brightspace, Zoom and YES are safe to use, even if prompted to authenticate. Personal accounts, such as Google, are also safe to use. All other Vanderbilt systems and applications remain restricted, including CampusPrint.
Vanderbilt-issued devices are safe to use. VUPS urges community members to contact VUIT if they notice suspicious activity.
According to a university statement last night, an update regarding the cybersecurity attack was planned for 9 a.m. CST. As of 9:09 a.m., no update has been sent.
The Hustler will share more information as it becomes available.
In an interview with The Hustler, VSG president Simran Fitzpatrick and vice president William Dean, both juniors, said they met with Vanderbilt Student Affairs to share frustrations and concerns regarding the handling of the cybersecurity attack. Fitzpatrick and Dean said they are working with administration to best support the student body.
“Students are concerned about the cyberattacks and extortion threats, particularly what information was stolen, how it may be used, and how it could affect them personally,” Fitzpatrick and Dean said. “We are frustrated by the university’s lack of clear communication, and our priority is ensuring that students receive timely updates and are not academically penalized for circumstances beyond their control.”
According to an 8:53 p.m. CST call with VUIT, Brightspace and YES are safe to access. OneDrive and Box remain compromised. VUIT advises students to refrain from signing in to any Microsoft services if prompted for credentials.
VUIT does not yet have a timeline for when the cybersecurity incident will be resolved. The university will provide the community with more updates by tomorrow at 9 a.m. CST.
“The cyberattack is like a building that just exploded and we are trying to gather the pieces,” a VUIT representative said.
Vanderbilt campus Wi-Fi is now available for use, according to a 7 p.m. university-wide email. Other systems and applications remain restricted. Students and faculty will receive further updates tomorrow at 9 a.m. CST.
In a separate mass text message, the university said to check social media and the Vanderbilt website for further updates. It did not clarify if email services will be restricted.
This story was updated Nov. 9, 2026, at 1:16 p.m. CST to include a statement from Vanderbilt University Public Safety.
Vanderbilt Wi-Fi networks have experienced a cybersecurity incident , according to the university and VUIT. VUIT has confirmed a breach to The Hustler. Faculty were notified first, with there being an hour and 36 minutes before students were notified.
In a 10:06 a.m. statement, Dean of the Blair School of Music Melissa Rose said VUIT suggested students log off the network.
“Everyone is following VU protocols and waiting for further instruction. VUIT is working on it. For now, we are simply asking everyone to stay off the network entirely until we know more,” Rose said.
Students reported VUIT staff entering classrooms across campus, alerting faculty that school-issued computers are not safe to use. VUIT has urged the Vanderbilt community to close all Microsoft Word documents, OneDrive and Dropbox folders.
In an 11:26 a.m. CST statement, VUIT is urging the community to shut down university-issued devices and remain vigilant.
“[VUIT] is actively investigating and working to contain the situation. We are asking all members of the university community to shut down university devices, disconnect from university WiFi and remain extremely vigilant,” the statement reads. “Take immediate action if you notice any unusual or suspicious activity.
At 11:45 a.m., Vanderbilt University AlertVU issued a message to the Vanderbilt community, urging the same statement.
“If you need immediate assistance, contact the IT service desk (615-343-9999) using a separate device,” the statement reads.
At 1:12 p.m. CST, the university issued a statement notify

articles.title_orig: NASA’s secret weapon in the lunar space race may be … procurement reform?
articles.title_zh: NASA’s secret weapon in the lunar space race may be … procurement reform?
articles.content_orig:
Senior NASA officials held a lengthy news conference last weekend, laying out a series of lunar contract awards, new contract opportunities, and mission decisions. They followed one after the other: landers, nuclear-powered rovers, scouting drones, power generation, storage, and communication satellites.
“Hopefully, we’re keeping industry on their toes trying to catch up to all the solicitations we’re doing,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, more than 90 minutes into the news conference. “This is what it takes to do the Moon Base in the timeline we have set forth.”
The rapid-fire announcement of awards tells us a few things about NASA’s efforts to return to the Moon and establish a durable settlement there during the next decade.
First, the agency is serious about this effort—the Artemis Moon Base program represents the most credible effort to establish a permanent outpost on another world in NASA’s history. Second, NASA is reaching out to all corners of the US commercial space industry, casting an extraordinarily wide net to reach companies that have yet to fly any hardware into orbit. Third, NASA is getting creative about how it’s buying these services, and this may matter most of all.
There was a lot packed into the announcements this weekend, so to make sense of it all, I called Mike Gold, a lawyer and former NASA associate administrator who set up the Artemis Accords, who is now the president of Redwire Space. He was at NASA at the beginning of Artemis and understands what it takes to get the government moving. He said he was blown away. During a period of seven days, Gold said, NASA put out five proposals for lunar contracts.
“The pace that’s occurring, and the nature of the procurements is unprecedented,” Gold said. “You are seeing an all-hands-on-deck approach. Big companies, small companies, new companies, old companies.”
What has impressed Gold most about NASA’s strategy since announcing the Moon Base in March, at the Ignition event , has been the agency’s evolving procurement strategy. The space agency has adopted a flexible procurement strategy similar to one used by the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.
There are two components. NASA has largely used a mechanism called Broad Agency Announcements, which ask for a capability such as providing power on the surface of the Moon. This allows NASA to ask industry for ideas without being too prescriptive and levying a bunch of requirements. It’s rather like instead of telling industry precisely what it wants, NASA asks industry what it can do.
Critically, Gold said, the space agency has also used a DARPA-style preliminary proposal process. In response to a traditional procurement, interested companies would prepare a detailed proposal, often running dozens, if not hundreds, of pages. This required an extraordinary amount of time.
With the Moon Base, NASA is employing a two-step process. After NASA announces the need for a service, interested companies submit a short white paper describing their solution. After a short review, NASA identifies the concepts it wants to pursue further, and only then do companies invest the time and resources to prepare a detailed proposal.
Gold said several lunar opportunities interested Redwire, and the company submitted initial proposals in response. But it only had to prepare a full proposal for opportunities that NASA wanted to pursue, including using a variant of its roll-out solar arrays on the Moon to generate power.
“We were able to focus the lion’s share of our resources in what the agency really wanted and what we were best at,” he said.
From this shift, it seems clear that NASA is trying to move away from micromanaging every individual lunar-base subsystem and instead seeks to coordinate independently developed commercial capabilities. The space agency is sourcing them from everywhere, from major contractors like Lockheed Martin, SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Northrop Grumman to relatively new startups such as Impulse Space, ispace-US, Voyager Technologies, Quantum Space, and more.
With questions emerging about how committed SpaceX is to NASA work in the future, the space agency appears to be seeking to diversify the way it gets cargo to the Moon. For example, it is leaning into Relativity Space and its large (but unproven) Terran R rocket, as well as orbital transfer vehicles built by Impulse Space. NASA is prioritizing the creation of a whole ecosystem of potential contractors rather than relying on one or two primes.
In doing so, NASA is taking a big risk. It is attempting to accelerate its lunar program by buying services from companies whose hardware is not yet operational and, in some cases, exists only as advanced engineering designs. For NASA, ultimately, it is a high-risk, high-reward approach. But in a demanding contest with China to reach and establish settlements on the Moon, NASA’s post-Apollo timidity is no longer tenable.
So how will NASA pay for all of the new stuff? Some of the funding is being repurposed from the previously shuttered Lunar Gateway program, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said. For example, as part of the “One Big Beautiful Bill” act passed in 2025, NASA received $2.6 billion for the Gateway. Some of the funding was already appropriated through the agency’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services Program.
Moreover, Isaacman said, some of these contracts are relatively small and will enable NASA to invest more down the road in successful services.
“By doing a lot of littles, and learning from our approach and also putting some good wins on the board, we’re demonstrating that we can be very efficient and responsible with taxpayer dollars,” he said. With this approach, he added, “You give future administrations the option of how they can dial up or down missions. Some of these missions in the, call it, $200 million range between launch, lander, and payload; potentially, you can add those or drop those inside a $25 billion approximate budget per year without putting the entire program at risk.”

articles.title_orig: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.title_zh: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.content_orig:
Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms
Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.
Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.
She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.
“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.
“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.
“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”
The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.
“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”
Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”
Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.
Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.
In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”
Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.
The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.
Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.
Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history , there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.
“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”
Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.
Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”
Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

articles.title_orig: AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents
articles.title_zh: AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents
articles.content_orig:
November 11, 2026 • 1671 words
In 2004, barely a month into my new job at Amazon, I got the opportunity to pick an intern to join my team. I had an advantage over my colleagues: I had already heard about a brilliant young man working toward his PhD at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam (where I happened to have received mine as well :-)). I immediately picked Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, whom you all now know as Swami. It was probably one of the best decisions I have made in my 22 years as Amazon’s CTO.
After a disastrous Christmas in 2004, when commercial relational databases could not scale to Amazon’s needs, I asked Swami to do a deep dive into how relational databases were actually used at Amazon. It turned out that 70% of database operations were not relational at all. They were key-value. That insight led to Dynamo , which Swami helped architect. When his internship was over, I hired him full-time right away, even before he had finished his PhD .
Bringing in another opinionated academic led to many fantastic discussions with Amazon’s practical engineers, who had become scale experts by actually building at scale. Eventual vs. strong consistency, CAP vs. Paxos, and more. Over time, Swami became one of the principal architects of AWS’s data strategy. And as we have seen in recent years, he has also been one of the intellectual drivers behind AI innovation at Amazon.
I am honoured that he wanted to write a guest post about the fundamental distributed systems work that sits behind many of AWS’s services, and about how the engineer’s work changes when agents write the code. AWS Emulator, launched today, gives agents the kind of test environment that work relied on. Swami’s story is another great example of invisible engineering .
Today we release AWS Emulator, which gives coding agents a local copy of AWS to test against, and it connects to a project from early in my career. In many ways, this emulator launch reminds me of the effort we put into reliable software engineering to improve the quality of the distributed systems we build. To that end, we wanted to share a story:
About twenty years ago, Werner asked me to work with one of Amazon’s earliest engineers, Al Vermeulen, on a distributed lock service we called “Alf”. Alf was built on Paxos, a protocol based on Leslie Lamport’s work that lets a group of servers agree on one value, and a replication engine in it kept copies of the data consistent across servers. Alf, to date, is the service that powers many of our complex distributed systems like S3, DynamoDB and many more (although it has evolved quite a bit with various changes on top â will save it for another blog!).
Paxos is the gold standard among distributed systems consensus protocols and was well understood in academia. However, building it at the scale Amazon and AWS were growing into was not easy. We had to deal with not just replication across servers and data centers but also tens of thousands of clients asking for locks at the same time, renewing their leases during network partitions all the while with the core requirement: Always be correct! At that time, the best ideas for testing distributed systems were large-scale system testing and chaos-based testing. Both worked, but they were expensive, and they could not reproduce many kinds of conditions on demand. That mattered for Alf, which was meant to be the truth store, giving every client a strongly consistent view of the truth, and which had to keep working through server failures and packet loss as well. Several industry papers had written that Paxos-based locking services were hard to get right, and the difficulty of testing them was part of the reason.
We addressed that by simulating Alf’s environment with as much fidelity as we could manage. We ran the servers inside a JVM and simulated the network and the rest of the infrastructure they depended on, so the whole system lived in one program that we controlled. We could drop packets and inject other faults whenever we chose, and we built tools that poked at the simulation for bugs and scalability problems. Concurrency bugs appear only when events happen in a particular order, and in the simulation we could set up many of those orderings on purpose and inspect how Alf handled each one. We also used formal reasoning, through theoretical techniques such as TLA+, and it found many issues as well. By testing this way we ironed out most of Alf’s concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing in a real environment then turned up different problems, because the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.
Simulation and formal reasoning both improved the software quality of the distributed systems we applied them to. The simulation worked because a small team could build a copy of one system’s environment by hand, and at the time AWS had only a small handful of services. But today AWS has over 200 services, and an application that calls AWS needs a test environment for each one it uses. Building all of those by hand would take years of engineering, and agents now write code far faster than any team can check it in production. So, we wanted to know whether agents could build and test those environments themselves.
The idea came from Matt Goldberg, a Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. His hypothesis was that, given a written description of how a service should behave and the real service to check against, an agent could build a working version of that service on its own. For AWS, the written description is the set of public API models, written in Smithy, AWS’s format for describing a service’s operations and their inputs, outputs, and errors. The real service to check against is the AWS cloud itself, the same system customers use.
The agents work from fidelity tests, which are end-to-end customer scenarios devised from the public API models. A test might check, for example, that in Amazon Simple Queue Service a received message stays hidden from other readers until its visibility timeout runs out. The agents correct each test until it passes against real AWS, so the test records how AWS behaves. The agents then build the emulator until it passes that same test, and a test that still fails points at a gap in the emulator. Matt began with SQS alone, and when he gave Kiro one prompt describing this approach, it returned a passable first version of an SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. Matt Goldbergâs launch post tells how that prototype grew into AWS Emulator. All of AWS Emulator’s code was written and tested by agents, and it is built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. It runs free and offline on your own machine. Teams of agents test it against real AWS and fix the gaps they find. Every change goes through a merge gate, a deep bench of automated checks that every change must pass before it enters the codebase, including several security agents doing adversarial reviews.
A coding agent works in a loop: it writes code, runs it, and reads the result before deciding what to change next. In distributed systems that loop runs inside infrastructure, so the services it calls have to behave like the real ones. When they do, an agent can check its own work as it writes and produce correct code on its first attempt far more often, which improves software quality. AWS Emulator puts that infrastructure inside the loop on your own machine.
When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct. It was a lesson I learned the hard way when I used Kiro to rebuild the replication engine that Al and I had built for Alf, which took us about four months the first time. I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to label Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat in a Situation Room confrontation last week that illustrates the tension inside the Trump administration over Chinese access to Nvidia’s advanced chips, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks. But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, also were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who the intelligence community suspected of being a Chinese spy, people familiar with the matter said.
But despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, the people said.
Confronted on it by Bessent last Thursday, Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
Axios first reported the Situation Room confrontation.
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Alice Huang became director and the company changed its name, it has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia , purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors, by some analyst estimates.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”
The entity list represents one of the US’s most significant tools for preventing American firms from selling their products to foreign companies and organizations. But adding Megaspeed to the list could also risk inflaming tensions with China amid Trump’s efforts to manage the US’ trade relationship with the fellow superpower. The Commerce Department hasn’t added any company to the list in more than a year.
Representatives for the Treasury and Commerce departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO could draw record retail buyers, Vanda Research says
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO could draw record retail buyers, Vanda Research says
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Everyday investors could pour a record $250 million into Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) shares on its first day of trading, according to Vanda Research.
The estimate, which would be more than double the $118 million in net retail buying the first day of SpaceX's ( SPCX ) June listing, hinges on a surge in derivatives trading tied to Anthropic's yet-to-be-listed shares on crypto exchange Hyperliquid.
Trading volume in this Anthropic-linked instrument reached a record $270 million on Tuesday, nearly triple last week's daily volumes, according to analysis from Vanda strategist Viraj Patel.
Vanda found that retail stock trading activity on the opening days of recent IPOs, including SpaceX, was roughly five times the peak daily trading volume in their pre-IPO derivatives. Based on Anthropic's Tuesday perpetual futures trading activity, the assessment would suggest $250 million in net buying on the company's planned listing day next week.
The projection comes with considerable caveats. The perpetual futures tied to Anthropic represent a speculative gauge of investor enthusiasm, and patterns from previous IPOs may not repeat.
Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $1.4 trillion, below the $2 trillion market value previously discussed, as the AI industry has faced headwinds from rising borrowing costs, hedge fund deleveraging, and political backlash over data center construction.
Anthropic is also planning a retail investor allocation of up to 20%, to be distributed through online brokerages, including US-based Charles Schwab ( SCHW ), Fidelity, Morgan Stanley's E-Trade, Robinhood ( HOOD ), and SoFi ( SOFI ).

articles.title_orig: No risk to public from hoax school bomb threats, says government minister
articles.title_zh: No risk to public from hoax school bomb threats, says government minister
articles.content_orig:
Scotland's education secretary has said there is no risk to the public after schools across the country were targeted with a fresh wave of hoax bomb threats, less than a month after a previous alert.
At least 1,000 schools received the hoax email, though police and the government said there was nothing within them to suggest a credible threat.
Government minister Mairi McAllan told parliament the situation was "very much in hand".
Specialist cyber-crime officers are working to identify the source of the messages, which were sent to both primary and secondary schools.
Similar "bogus" emails were sent to 300 schools in Northern Ireland , while schools in Italy also received threats.
Assistant Chief Constable Mark Sutherland told the BBC Scotland News that the police were able to assess the threat as a hoax in around an hour and urged parents not to keep their children away from school.
He said: "First and foremost, I'll be sending my daughter to school tomorrow. I think what is important is that we continue to be vigilant, but we are not alarmed.
"We have carried out a significant amount of checks on all of the information we have gathered so far and there is nothing to suggest there is a credible threat and there is no requirement to keep children away from education settings."
He said officers believed that the email was sent by the same source as emails sent to schools in Northern Ireland and elsewhere in the UK but it was "too early to say" who could be behind it.
"We will be working with partners across the UK and internationally to carry out a joined-up investigation," he added.
The education secretary told MSPs that she had held a meeting with police and local authorities.
"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," Mairi McAllan said.
"I would take this opportunity to repeat Police Scotland's advice that there is nothing to suggest any threats to the public from the content of the emails."
The cabinet secretary added there was a "considerable amount of work" ongoing by Police Scotland and partners across the UK to "understand the motivations and the individuals behind this".
Most local authorities contacted by BBC Scotland said schools were operating as normal but some confirmed pupils had been evacuated.
More than 300 calls were made to police when a similar message was sent to schools around the country on 19 October.
In many areas, pupils were off due to half-term holidays.
On Wednesday the majority of schools in Dumfries and Galloway received the email and some were evacuated as a precaution.
A spokesperson for the local authority said: "Each school community/setting is unique and as such has its own way of supporting and reassuring learners and staff.
"We also know that local police have attended some school settings in a community capacity to assist and reassure."
In Edinburgh Queensferry High School was evacuated and pupils were sent home.
Highland Council confirmed a number of its schools "made the decision to activate their emergency protocols".
Local authorities in Glasgow, Edinburgh, East Lothian, Aberdeenshire and Orkney also confirmed their schools received the message.
In Northern Ireland, the Education Authority (EA) said the "message has similarities with a bogus threat sent last month" which was treated as a hoax by the (PSNI).
The Police Service of Northern Ireland said the email originated from outside the UK .
Italian reports said 280 school head teachers had received threats in recent days. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has called a meeting of top ministers and intelligence chiefs over the issue.

Popular VoIP app Google Voice is laying the groundwork for RCS (Rich Communication Services) messaging, we can exclusively reveal. Google Voice users are currently limited to standard SMS and MMS, a glaring limitation at a time when multiple apps, including Google Messages, already support RCS messaging. It looks like the company may finally fix this in a forthcoming update.
You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.
Looking at version 2026.11.01.10 of Google Voice, we uncovered evidence suggesting RCS support is coming to the service. One of the strings we found specifically references the ability to toggle RCS chats.
We’re also getting a look at other strings that mention more RCS-related actions, as shown in the screenshot below.
Lastly, another string tells us that an RCS label would appear in the compose box, similar to existing labels for SMS and MMS.
The fact that RCS messaging isn’t supported on Google Voice already has baffled many users over the years, including our very own .
It finally looks like Google is taking steps to address this missing feature, although it’s difficult to say when that may happen. Since we only have references in the app’s code and no actual visuals, it could be a while before RCS messaging goes live in Google Voice.
There’s also the chance that Google may not implement it, though we hope that’s not the case. Bringing RCS support to Google Voice messaging would finally enable end-to-end encryption, read receipts, and high-resolution media sharing, among other benefits.

articles.title_orig: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement - International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.title_zh: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement - International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.content_orig:
November 11, 2026 | By: Zhihang Meng, Hae Jeong Cho, Yuanrong Zhou, Gabriel Hillman Alvarez, Jakob Schmidt
Maritime shipping plays a key role in China’s national freight sector, accounting for over 50% of transportation activity in 2024. Decarbonization of this sector at a rate in line with the government’s goal to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060 will require the large-scale application of ships fueled by low- and zero-carbon fuels.
China introduced policies in 2024 to promote the scrapping and renewal of old ships, which offer shipowners tiered subsidies to renew older ships before their mandatory retirement dates, with greater support for new/clean energy vessels (NCEVs). However, the policy does not specify which fuels NCEVs must use.
This paper estimates the potential impact of the retire-and-renew (RNR) policy on fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions in China’s coastal fleet. Using the Vessel Economic Guidance and Assessment (VEGA) model and Polaris, a shipping emissions projection model, we estimated fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions from 2025 to 2050 under the existing RNR policy design and two alternative scenarios.
